To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

PCV7 vaccination in the first 12 months of life does not eliminate carriage of PCV7 vaccine serotypes in the nasopharengal swab of children, and that the frequency and duration of PCV7 carriage increases with time from vaccination.

(i) the majority of children in this highly vaccinated cohort are colonized by pneumococcal strains; (ii) pneumococcal colonizers are frequently co-carriers of more than one serotype, with a total of 33 serotypes detected in 1,728 pneumococcal isolates; (iii) PCV7 serotyping is found in children who have received >2 doses of PCVs in the first year and in the following years; and (iv)
PCV7 vaccination does not reduce the carriage of pneumococci and that PCV7 vaccinated subjects can carry PCV7 serogroups, especially in the years following vaccination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long term impact of PCV7 vaccination on nasopharyngealn colonization.
the long-term impact of vaccination with 7-valent conjugate vaccine on pneumococci colonization patterns.
the impact of the 7 valent pneumococccal vaccine on pneumococci serotypes carriage in a cohort of highly vaccinated children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of PCV7 has not significantly changed the carriage patterns in this highly vaccinated Italian population.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PCV7 is not a magic bullet against pneumococcal carriage.
PCV7 has a limited impact on pneumococci carriage and that PCV7 vaccination does not prevent colonization with PCV7 serotypic strains.
PCV7 vaccination is not able to eradicate pneumococci from the nasopharynges of vaccinated children and that PCV7 coverage is lower than expected.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PCV7 vaccination has not been able to eliminate the carriage of pneumococcal disease-causing serotypes.
PCV7 is not a panacea against pneumococcal carriage.
the use of RT-PCR to detect S. pneumoniae serotypes in nasopharynx swabs is a valid method to evaluate the impact of pneumococcal vaccination on pneumococci carriage.
